name: JavaFX
summary: A Java desktop UI toolkit that represents interfaces as a constrained scene graph, exposes observable properties and event dispatch, and renders attached scenes through a platform runtime and pulse-driven toolkit.

features.name: Constrained scene graph
features.description: JavaFX Node and Parent define a tree in which nodes have at most one parent, branch nodes own children, cycles are rejected, and nodes attached to a showing Scene are modified on the JavaFX Application Thread.
benefits: Makes containment and display eligibility explicit
Enables traversal, layout, styling, and rendering over one hierarchy
costs: Single-parent and no-cycle rules constrain composition

features.name: Observable property and binding model
features.description: The javafx.beans property and binding APIs expose mutable and read-only properties, listeners, and derived bindings so state changes can notify dependent UI objects.
benefits: Supports one-way and derived state relationships
costs: Listener lifetime and invalidation ordering require discipline
Binding graphs can add update work

features.name: Pulse-driven rendering runtime
features.description: The JavaFX toolkit schedules scene processing and rendering through a runtime pulse, separating application-thread scene mutation from toolkit-level synchronization and rendering work.
benefits: Batches layout, CSS, animation, and rendering work around frames
Provides a common runtime boundary for platform windows
costs: Visible updates depend on pulse scheduling
Application-thread and toolkit timing are additional correctness constraints

mathematical_views.model: Rooted scene graph with ownership constraints
mathematical_views.question: How do parent-child edges, single ownership, and acyclicity constrain the set of nodes eligible for display?
assumptions: Nodes and parent-child edges form a forest
Scene attachment marks a display-relevant root
The view abstracts layout and rendering algorithms

mathematical_views.model: Observable dependency graph and pulse state machine
mathematical_views.question: How do property invalidations become scheduled scene updates and eventually a rendered frame?
assumptions: Properties and bindings form dependency edges
Invalidation schedules work rather than proving immediate rendering
A pulse is modeled as a transition that processes pending work

costs: Reparenting and mutation rules are strict
Dependency and listener graphs need lifecycle management
Scheduling and thread boundaries affect latency
